questions.stemText:
A transmitting aerial emits vertically polarised radio waves. A receiving aerial is positioned at an angle $\theta$ from the horizontal and is in the plane perpendicular to the direction of plane-polarised waves. The amplitude of the wave received is $A$.

Which of the following is the total power of the transmitting aerial directly proportional to?

A $A^2\cos^2\theta$
B $\frac{A^2}{\cos^2\theta}$
C $A^2\sin^2\theta$
D $\frac{A^2}{\sin^2\theta}$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: A transmitting aerial emits vertically polarised radio waves. A receiving aerial is positioned at an angle θ from the horizontal and is in the plane perpendicul

appearances.originalFile: grail:9605 ACJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must undo the vertical projection and square the recovered amplitude.
questions.misconception: Taking the angle from the wrong axis

explanation.body: With transmitted amplitude $A_0$, the receiving aerial measures $A=A_0\sin\theta$. The received power and intensity are proportional to $A^2=A_0^2\sin^2\theta$. The transmitted power and intensity are proportional to $A_0^2=A^2/\sin^2\theta$.

perOption.A: Uses a horizontal projection and applies it again to the received amplitude.
perOption.B: Uses cosine as though the angle were measured from the vertical.
perOption.C: Projects the received amplitude again instead of recovering the transmitted amplitude.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Two identical water waves travel from two sources X and Y to meet at point P. The frequency of the waves is $0.40\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and the sources are in phase.

[Two arrows point from source X and source Y toward P.]

Waves from source X take $3.0\ \mathrm{s}$ to arrive at P, while waves from source Y take $3.5\ \mathrm{s}$ to arrive at P.

What is the phase difference, in radians, between the two waves at P?

A $\pi/5$
B $2\pi/5$
C $5\pi/2$
D $5\pi$

stemImage.alt: Question 17: Two identical water waves travel from two sources X and Y to meet at point P. The frequency of the waves is 0.40 Hz and the sources are in phase. Waves from sou

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must turn a travel-time difference into a fraction of a cycle.
questions.misconception: Using half a cycle as the radian conversion factor

explanation.body: The travel-time difference is $3.5-3.0=0.5\ \mathrm{s}$. Each cycle is $2\pi$ radians, so the phase difference is $2\pi f\Delta t=2\pi(0.40)(0.5)=2\pi/5$ radians.

perOption.A: Uses $\pi$ radians for a full cycle.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: This is the numerical value of the period in seconds, $5/2$, multiplied by $\pi$.
perOption.D: Uses the numerical value of the period, 2.5, as the number of cycles in the phase calculation.

questions.difficultyReason: The student counts compression intervals and substitutes into the wave equation.
questions.misconception: Treating a compression-to-rarefaction interval as a wavelength

explanation.body: One wavelength is the distance between adjacent compressions. The $100\ \mathrm{m}$ span contains five wavelengths, so $\lambda=100/5=20\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $v=f\lambda$ gives $350=20f$, so $f\approx18\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Uses twice the compression-to-compression spacing as the wavelength.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the compression-to-rarefaction spacing as a full wavelength.
perOption.D: Implies a sub-metre wavelength, whereas adjacent compressions are 20 m apart.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The frequency of a water wave is $400\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and its speed is $36\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

What is the phase difference between the motions of two points on the wave that are $0.18\ \mathrm{m}$ apart?

A $0.50\pi$
B $1.0\pi$
C $2.0\pi$
D $2.5\pi$

stemImage.alt: Question 18: The frequency of a water wave is 400 Hz and its speed is 36 m s─1. What is the phase difference between the motions of two points on the wave that are 0.18 m ap

appearances.originalFile: grail:14529 (ACJC) 2024 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student calculates the wavelength and recognises when a whole-cycle phase difference is equivalent.
questions.misconception: Treating equivalent whole-cycle phases as distinct

explanation.body: The wavelength is $\lambda=v/f=36/400=0.090\ \mathrm{m}$. Using $\Delta x/\lambda=\Delta\phi/(2\pi)$ gives $\Delta\phi=[0.18/(36/400)](2\pi)=4\pi$. This is equivalent to the listed phase difference of $2\pi$, since both describe points in phase.

perOption.A: $0.50\pi$ represents a quarter-cycle phase offset.
perOption.B: This gives half a cycle, whereas the two points are in phase.
perOption.C: Correct. It is equivalent to the calculated two complete cycles.
perOption.D: $2.5\pi$ leaves a quarter-cycle offset after one full cycle is removed.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A progressive longitudinal sound wave moves through air. P, Q, R, S and T are the positions of the air particles along part of the wave at one instant.

[Ten dots lie on a horizontal line. The first three are close together with P at the middle dot. Q labels the fourth dot, the fifth is unlabelled and R labels the sixth. Dots seven to nine are close together with S at the middle dot, and T labels the tenth dot. Q, the fifth dot and R are widely and evenly spaced.]

Which pair of particles has a phase difference of $\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$?

A P and S
B P and T
C Q and R
D R and S

stemImage.alt: Question 14: A progressive longitudinal sound wave moves through air. P, Q, R, S and T are the positions of the air particles along part of the wave at one instant. Which pa

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify opposite phases from particle spacing in a longitudinal wave.
questions.misconception: Confusing successive compressions with opposite phases.

explanation.body: P and S are at the centres of compressions, while T is at the centre of a rarefaction. A compression centre and a rarefaction centre differ in phase by $\pi\ \mathrm{rad}$, so P and T have that phase difference.

perOption.A: P and S are both compression centres, so they are in phase.
perOption.B: Correct. P is at a compression centre and T is at a rarefaction centre.
perOption.C: Mistakes the relatively wide spacing between Q and R for a half-cycle separation.
perOption.D: R is between a rarefaction centre and the compression centred at S, so the pair is less than half a cycle apart.

questions.stemText:
A microphone and a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) are used to analyse a sound wave. The trace is displayed on the screen of the CRO as shown.

[The CRO grid shows a sinusoidal trace over six major horizontal divisions, with a dashed centreline. The first and second troughs are at one and five divisions from the left edge, and the crest is at three divisions. One major division is marked $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ on both axes.]

The speed of sound is $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and the CRO has a time-base setting of $4.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s\,cm^{-1}}$.

What is the wavelength of the sound wave?

A $1.3\ \mathrm{cm}$
B $2.6\ \mathrm{cm}$
C $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$
D $5.3\ \mathrm{cm}$

stemImage.alt: Question 15: A microphone and a cathode-ray oscilloscope (CRO) are used to analyse a sound wave. The trace is displayed on the screen of the CRO as shown. The speed of sound

appearances.originalFile: grail:19926 ACJC 2025 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must read a full cycle, apply the time-base scale and convert the frequency into a wavelength.
questions.misconception: Treating the horizontal trace as distance travelled by the sound.

explanation.body: One full cycle spans $4.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ on the screen, giving $T=4(4.0\times10^{-5})=1.6\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm s$. The frequency is $f=1/T=6250\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Hence $\lambda=v/f=330/6250=5.3\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Uses one horizontal division for a whole cycle.
perOption.B: Uses two horizontal divisions, which span only half a cycle.
perOption.C: Reads the width of a cycle on the screen as a physical wavelength in air.
perOption.D: Correct. The full-cycle time gives a wavelength of $5.3\ \mathrm{cm}$.

A second wave of similar type has twice the intensity and half the frequency.

When drawn on the same axes, which graph would the second wave look like?
questions.stemText: A displacement-time graph is shown for a particular wave. A second wave of similar type has twice the intensity and half the frequency. When drawn on the same axes, which graph would the second wave look like? A  B  C  D

questions.difficultyReason: Two simultaneous changes (amplitude via intensity ∝ A², and period) must be read off grids.
questions.misconception: Thinking amplitude is proportional to intensity rather than its square root

explanation.body:
Intensity $\propto$ amplitude$^2$, so twice the intensity means the amplitude is $\sqrt{2}$ times larger.

Half the frequency means the period is doubled, so the graph shows half as many cycles.

perOption.A: Doubles the amplitude, as if intensity were proportional to amplitude.
perOption.B: Correct. Amplitude $\times\sqrt{2}$ and period doubled.
perOption.C: Doubles the amplitude and doubles the frequency instead of halving it.
perOption.D: Correct amplitude, but the frequency is doubled instead of halved.

The graph shows the shape at a particular instant of part of a transverse wave travelling along a string.

Which statement about the motion of points in the string is correct?
questions.stemText: The graph shows the shape at a particular instant of part of a transverse wave travelling along a string. Which statement about the motion of points in the string is correct? A The speed at point P is a maximum. B The displacement at point Q is always zero. C The energy at point R is entirely kinetic. D The acceleration at point S is a maximum.

options.label: A
options.text: The speed at point P is a maximum.

options.label: B
options.text: The displacement at point Q is always zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The energy at point R is entirely kinetic.

options.label: D
options.text: The acceleration at point S is a maximum.

appearances.originalFile: grail:9611 ASRJC 2022 Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer instantaneous motion from a spatial snapshot.
questions.misconception: Treating a zero crossing as a fixed node

explanation.body: P is at a crest and its transverse speed is zero. The displacement of Q varies sinusoidally with time. At the trough R the speed is zero, so its kinetic energy is zero. At S the displacement is greatest in magnitude, and $a=-\omega^2x$ gives the greatest acceleration magnitude.

perOption.A: P is at a crest where its transverse speed is zero.
perOption.B: Q passes through equilibrium and continues to oscillate.
perOption.C: R has zero transverse speed at the trough, so its kinetic energy is zero.
perOption.D: Correct. S has maximum acceleration magnitude.

questions.stemText: When plane-polarised light of amplitude a is passed through a polarising filter as shown, the amplitude of the light emerging is a cos θ. The intensity of the initial beam is I. What is the intensity of the emerging light when θ is 60.0o? A 0.250 I B 0.500 I C 0.750 I D 0.866 I

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The amplitude ratio is given by one cosine and must be squared to obtain the intensity ratio.
questions.misconception: Treating intensity as proportional to amplitude.

explanation.body: Intensity is proportional to amplitude squared, so $\frac{I}{I_1}=\frac{a^2}{a_1^2}$. With $a_1=a\cos 60.0^\circ=0.500a$, the emerging intensity is $I_1=\frac{(0.500a)^2}{a^2}I=0.250I$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the amplitude ratio directly as the intensity ratio.
perOption.C: Uses the squared sine, which gives the fraction associated with the blocked component.
perOption.D: Uses the sine of the angle as the intensity ratio.

The lower row represents the same particles at one instant as a longitudinal wave passes from left to right through the Earth. What should be measured to determine the amplitude of the oscillations of the particles in the lower row as the wave passes? A half the maximum displacement of the particles from their position at rest B half the maximum distance apart of the particles C the maximum displacement of the particles from their position at rest D the maximum distance apart of the particles

options.label: B

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires applying the definition of amplitude to the two rows.
questions.misconception: Confusing particle spacing with particle displacement.

explanation.body: Amplitude is the maximum magnitude of a particle’s displacement from its rest position. Compare the positions of corresponding bars in the two rows and take the largest shift.

perOption.A: Halves a displacement already measured from equilibrium.
perOption.B: Uses half the spacing between particles as if it were half a peak-to-peak displacement.

perOption.D: Measures separation between particles instead of displacement from each particle’s rest position.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
As the intensity of a single frequency sound wave travelling through the air is increased, how do the maximum speed of vibration of the air molecules and the speed of wave travel change?

[Table columns in order: maximum speed of vibration of air molecules, speed of wave travel.]
A increase, increase
B increase, no change
C no change, increase
D no change, no change

stemImage.alt: Question 15: As the intensity of a single frequency sound wave travelling through the air is increased, how do the maximum speed of vibration of the air molecules and the sp

appearances.originalFile: grail:18733 ASRJC 2025 Prelim P1 H2 Physics QN paper

questions.difficultyReason: It links intensity to particle amplitude and distinguishes particle speed from wave speed.
questions.misconception: Confusing particle speed with wave speed.

explanation.body: The air molecules undergo simple harmonic motion. Wave intensity is proportional to the square of the displacement amplitude $x_0$, so raising the intensity increases $x_0$ and hence the maximum molecular speed $v_0=(2\pi f)x_0$. The speed of sound is set by the properties of the air, which are unchanged.

perOption.A: Assumes greater intensity also makes the wave travel faster.
perOption.B: Correct. The molecular speed increases and the wave speed stays fixed.
perOption.C: Keeps molecular speed fixed despite the larger amplitude and incorrectly increases wave speed.
perOption.D: Overlooks the increase in molecular speed at fixed frequency.

A At P, the air pressure is minimum. B At Q, it is a position of antinode. C At Q, the air molecule is momentarily at rest. D At P, the air molecule is moving in the positive x-direction.

options.label: B
options.text: At Q, it is a position of antinode.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires linking compressions/rarefactions in a progressive longitudinal wave to pressure and particle velocity.
questions.misconception: Applying standing-wave terms (nodes, antinodes) to a progressive wave; thinking molecules at a rarefaction are at rest

explanation.body: At P, the displacement curve crosses zero with a negative slope. As the curve shifts right, the displacement at P becomes positive, so the particle is moving in the positive $x$-direction.

perOption.A: P is at a compression, where the pressure is maximum.
perOption.B: This is a progressive wave, so it has no stationary-wave antinodes.
perOption.C: At Q, the particle passes through equilibrium in a rarefaction at maximum speed.
perOption.D: Correct. The particle at P moves in the positive $x$-direction.

questions.difficultyReason: Students calculate the wavelength and relate it to the separation between opposite pressure extrema.
questions.misconception: Confusing the distance between opposite pressure extrema with a full wavelength

explanation.body: The nearest compression (maximum pressure) and rarefaction (minimum pressure) are half a wavelength apart. The wavelength is $\lambda=v/f=1500/2500=0.60\ \mathrm{m}$, so the distance is $\lambda/2=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: A quarter wavelength reaches the mean pressure.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: A full wavelength reaches the next pressure maximum.
perOption.D: Two wavelengths reach another pressure maximum.

questions.stem:
A narrow, parallel beam of unpolarised light is directed towards three ideal polarising filters.

The beam meets the first filter with a vertical axis of polarisation and emerges with an intensity Io. The axis of polarisation of the second filter is at an angle of 10° to the first filter. The third filter has its axis of polarization parallel to the second filter as shown.

The third filter is now turned an angle of 34° to the second filter. What is the intensity of the transmitted light after passing through the third filter?
questions.stemText: A narrow, parallel beam of unpolarised light is directed towards three ideal polarising filters. The beam meets the first filter with a vertical axis of polarisation and emerges with an intensity Io. The axis of polarisation of the second filter is at an angle of 10° to the first filter. The third filter has its axis of polarization parallel to the second filter as shown. 0° 10° Io 10° The third filter is now turned an angle of 34° to the second filter. What is the intensity of the transmitted light after passing through the third filter? A 0.25 $I_{\mathrm{o}}$ B 0.33 $I_{\mathrm{o}}$ C 0.5 $I_{\mathrm{o}}$ D 0.67 $I_{\mathrm{o}}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Students apply Malus’ law twice using successive axis angles.
questions.misconception: Applying Malus’ law using the first and last axes only

explanation.body: By Malus’ law, the intensity after the second filter is $I_2=I_0\cos^2 10^\circ$. The angle between the second and third axes is now $34^\circ$, so $I_3=I_2\cos^2 34^\circ=I_0\cos^2 10^\circ\cos^2 34^\circ=0.67I_0$.

perOption.A: Halving the intensity at each remaining filter ignores their relative axis angles.
perOption.B: Halving the result again would count the first filter twice, since the given intensity is already measured after it.
perOption.C: Using the combined angle of 44° skips the change of polarisation at the second filter.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stemText:
A transverse water wave is moving along the surface of some water. This causes a ball to move vertically without moving horizontally as it floats upon the surface. At one instant, the ball is at the position shown.

[Not-to-scale diagram of a rightward-travelling wave with a ball on the left crest, a vertical distance of $0.70\ \mathrm{m}$ from the equilibrium line to a crest, and a horizontal distance of $2.4\ \mathrm{m}$ from a trough to the next crest.]

The wave has a frequency of $0.20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ and an amplitude of $0.70\ \mathrm{m}$. The distance between a trough and an adjacent peak is $2.4\ \mathrm{m}$.

What is the distance travelled by the ball in a time of $20\ \mathrm{s}$?

A $5.6\ \mathrm{m}$; B $9.6\ \mathrm{m}$; C $11.2\ \mathrm{m}$; D $19.2\ \mathrm{m}$

stemImage.alt: Question 16: A transverse water wave is moving along the surface of some water. This causes a ball to move vertically without moving horizontally as it floats upon the surfa

questions.difficultyReason: The student combines the number of periods with the vertical distance per cycle.
questions.misconception: Confusing motion of the medium with wave propagation

explanation.body: The wave period is $T=1/f=5\ \mathrm{s}$, so the ball completes $20/5=4$ cycles. In each cycle the ball travels four amplitudes, giving a total distance of $4(0.70\times4)=11.2\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Counts only the crest-to-trough distance in each cycle.
perOption.B: Uses the horizontal trough-to-crest spacing as the distance the ball travels per cycle.

perOption.D: Uses the wave speed $f\lambda$ times the elapsed time.

What is the amplitude of the light at Q?
questions.stemText: A narrow, parallel beam of unpolarised light is passed through two optical polarisers. The first polariser’s transmission axis is oriented at 60° to the vertical, while the second polariser’s transmission axis is oriented at 45° to the horizontal. The light at P has amplitude A. What is the amplitude of the light at Q? A A cos 15° B A cos 45° C A cos 60° D A cos 75°

appearances.originalFile: grail:14541 CJC 2024.H2.Phy.PRELIM.P1 - QP

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation is a single amplitude projection after the angle between the two axes is read from the diagram.
questions.misconception: Using an angle measured from a reference line as the angle between the polarisers

explanation.body: The light at P is polarised along the first transmission axis, which makes an angle $180^\circ-(60^\circ+45^\circ)=75^\circ$ with the second transmission axis. Projecting the amplitude onto the second axis gives $A\cos75^\circ$ at Q.

perOption.A: Treats the two axes as sloping in the same direction and uses $15^\circ$.
perOption.B: Uses the second axis’s angle to the horizontal.
perOption.C: Uses the first axis’s angle to the vertical.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics

questions.difficultyReason: The student must count the distance in a full cycle and calculate the remaining motion from the oscillation phase.
questions.misconception: Confusing displacement from equilibrium with total distance

explanation.body:
The period is $T=1/f=1/1.50\approx0.67\ \mathrm{s}$. Starting at the crest gives $x=x_0\cos\omega t$, so at $0.75\ \mathrm{s}$ the displacement is $0.120\cos[(2\pi)(1.50)(0.75)]\approx0.08485\ \mathrm{m}$, or about $85\ \mathrm{mm}$.

P travels four amplitudes in the first cycle and then moves down from $120$ to $85\ \mathrm{mm}$, giving $4(120)+(120-85)=515\ \mathrm{mm}$.

perOption.B: Gives the final displacement from equilibrium instead of the accumulated distance.
perOption.C: Undercounts the completed cycle, which alone contributes $480\ \mathrm{mm}$.
perOption.D: Correct. The full cycle and the final partial cycle give $515\ \mathrm{mm}$.

questions.stemText:
A sound wave travelling towards the right through air causes the air molecules to be displaced from their original positions. The graph below shows the variation with distance of the displacement of air molecules at a particular instant of time.

[Graph of displacement against distance: a sinusoid starting at the origin, rising to a crest, falling through zero at A, reaching a trough at B, rising through zero at C, reaching a crest at D, then falling to another trough.]

Taking the displacement towards the right as positive, at which point is the pressure minimum?

A  A
B  B
C  C
D  D

stemImage.alt: Question 11: A sound wave travelling towards the right through air causes the air molecules to be displaced from their original positions. The graph below shows the variatio

appearances.originalFile: grail:15121 TMJC_2024_H2 Physics P1_QP_AS

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting a displacement–distance graph of a longitudinal wave into compressions and rarefactions, which many students find unintuitive.
questions.misconception: Thinking pressure is extreme where displacement is maximum

explanation.body:
Taking displacement to the right as positive: molecules with positive displacement have moved right, those with negative displacement have moved left.

Just to the left of C (around B) the displacement is negative, so molecules move to the left; just to the right of C the displacement is positive, so molecules move to the right. Molecules move away from C on both sides, so C is the centre of a rarefaction.

Hence C has the minimum pressure.

perOption.A: At A, molecules on the left are displaced right and those on the right are displaced left, so A is a compression (maximum pressure).
perOption.B: B has maximum displacement but zero displacement gradient, so the pressure there is at its normal (undisturbed) value.
perOption.C: Correct. Molecules on both sides are displaced away from C, giving a rarefaction.
perOption.D: D has maximum displacement but the pressure there is at its undisturbed value, not a minimum.

The frequency of the sound is 2 kHz. Which time-base setting on the oscilloscope will be appropriate?
questions.stemText: A student is investigating the frequency of a sound wave by using a microphone connected to a cathode-ray oscilloscope (C.R.O.) as shown below. C.R.O. microphone 1 cm 1 cm The frequency of the sound is 2 kHz. Which time-base setting on the oscilloscope will be appropriate? A 10 ms $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ B 0.1 ms $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ C 1 μs $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$ D 10 ns $\mathrm{cm}^{-1}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:19911 TMJC_2025_H2 Physics_P1_QP

questions.difficultyReason: Requires converting frequency to period and comparing with the screen width, with some prefix handling.
questions.misconception: Choosing a time-base without checking how many cycles fit on the screen

explanation.body:
A frequency of $2\ \mathrm{kHz}$ has a period of $T = 1/f = 0.5\ \mathrm{ms}$.

A typical C.R.O. screen has 10 horizontal divisions of $1\ \mathrm{cm}$ each. With a time-base of $0.1\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$, one period spans $0.5/0.1 = 5$ divisions, so two full cycles fill the screen.

perOption.A: At $10\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}$ one period is only $0.05\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide, so about 200 cycles are crammed onto the screen.
perOption.B: Correct. One period spans 5 cm, so two clear cycles fit on the 10 cm screen.
perOption.C: At $1\ \mathrm{\mu s\,cm^{-1}}$ one period would be $500\ \mathrm{cm}$ wide, so the screen shows only a tiny fraction of a cycle.
perOption.D: At $10\ \mathrm{ns\,cm^{-1}}$ the screen spans only $100\ \mathrm{ns}$, a minute fraction of the $0.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ period.

questions.difficultyReason: Conceptual: phase difference between fixed points on a progressive wave is constant.
questions.misconception: Confusing phase difference with displacement varying in time

explanation.body:
The phase difference between two points on a progressive wave is $\phi = \dfrac{x}{\lambda}\times 2\pi$, where $x$ is their fixed separation.

Since $x$ and $\lambda$ do not change, $\phi$ is independent of $t$: the graph is a horizontal line at a constant non-zero value.

perOption.B: Also a time-varying curve; phase difference between two fixed points is constant.

questions.stem:
A beam of vertically polarised light is incident normally on a polarising filter. The filter can be rotated so that it is always in a plane perpendicular to the beam. The transmission axis of the filter is initially vertical.

The filter is first rotated clockwise by an angle of $30^{\mathrm{o}}$ so that the transmitted light waves have intensity $I_{30}$. The filter is then rotated clockwise by a further angle of $30^{\mathrm{o}}$.

What is the new intensity of the transmitted light waves?
questions.stemText: A beam of vertically polarised light is incident normally on a polarising filter. The filter can be rotated so that it is always in a plane perpendicular to the beam. The transmission axis of the filter is initially vertical. The filter is first rotated clockwise by an angle of 30o so that the transmitted light waves have intensity I30. The filter is then rotated clockwise by a further angle of 30o. What is the new intensity of the transmitted light waves? A $0.25I_{30}$ B $0.33I_{30}$ C $0.75I_{30}$ D $0.87I_{30}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:19928 VJC 2025 J2 H2 Phy Prelim Paper 1

questions.difficultyReason: Requires measuring the total angle from the original polarisation and expressing the answer relative to I30.
questions.misconception: Applying Malus' law to the incremental 30° rotation instead of the total angle

explanation.body:
Let $I_0$ be the intensity of the incident light. By Malus' law:

$I_{30} = I_0\cos^2 30^\circ = 0.75I_0$

$I_{60} = I_0\cos^2 60^\circ = 0.25I_0$

Comparing, $I_{60} = \dfrac{0.25}{0.75}I_{30} = 0.33I_{30}$.

perOption.A: Gives $I_{60}$ as a fraction of $I_0$, not of $I_{30}$.
perOption.B: Correct. $\cos^2 60^\circ/\cos^2 30^\circ = 1/3$.
perOption.C: This is $I_{30}/I_0$; also treats the second rotation as relative to the first transmitted light rather than the original vertical polarisation.
perOption.D: Uses $\cos\theta$ instead of $\cos^2\theta$ for intensity.

questions.stemText: The diagram shows the displacement of a transverse wave along a stretched cord at a particular instant. The wave travels from left to right with frequency 20 Hz. What is the shortest time before the displacement at Q becomes zero? A 6.25 ms B 18.8 ms C 31.3 ms D 43.8 ms

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The student must use the direction of travel to identify which zero crossing will reach Q first.
questions.misconception: Using the nearest crossing on the wrong side of Q.

explanation.body: The period is $T=1/f=1/20\ \mathrm{s}=50\ \mathrm{ms}$. The wavelength spans eight divisions, and the right-moving zero crossing immediately to the left of Q is one division away. This is a phase difference of $\Delta\phi=2\pi/8=\pi/4$, so $\Delta t=(\Delta\phi/2\pi)T=6.25\ \mathrm{ms}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The first zero crossing reaches Q in one eighth of a period.
perOption.B: Uses the zero crossing three divisions to the right of Q, which moves away.
perOption.C: Uses the second zero crossing to arrive, five divisions to the left of Q.
perOption.D: Uses seven eighths of a period for a shift of only one division.

questions.stemText: Two polarising filters, P and Q, are placed in front of a light sensor. Their transmission axes are initially parallel. Unpolarised light passes through them and the sensor records an intensity I. Filter Q is then rotated while filter P remains fixed. Which angle through which Q may be rotated would reduce the detected intensity by 36%? A 23⁰ B 37⁰ C 50⁰ D 53⁰

appearances.originalFile: VJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires converting the percentage reduction to a transmitted fraction before applying Malus’ law.
questions.misconception: Using the percentage lost as the percentage transmitted.

explanation.body: By Malus’ law the detected intensity is $I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $I_0$ is the reading for parallel axes. A 36% reduction leaves $0.64I_0$, so $\cos^2\theta=0.64$. This gives $\theta=36.9^\circ$, or about $37^\circ$.

perOption.A: Transmits about 85% of the original reading, a drop of only about 15%.
perOption.B: Correct. About 64% of the original reading remains.
perOption.C: Transmits about 41% of the original reading, a drop of about 59%.
perOption.D: Treats the 36% lost as the fraction transmitted.

questions.stem: A wave of frequency 15 Hz travels at 24 m $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ through a medium. What is the phase difference between two points 2.0 m apart?
questions.stemText: A wave of frequency 15 Hz travels at 24 m s–1 through a medium. What is the phase difference between two points 2.0 m apart? A There is no phase difference. B They are out of phase by a quarter of a cycle. C They are out of phase by half of a cycle. D They are out of phase by 0.80 of a cycle.

options.label: B
options.text: They are out of phase by a quarter of a cycle.

options.label: C
options.text: They are out of phase by half of a cycle.

options.label: D
options.text: They are out of phase by 0.80 of a cycle.

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Computing wavelength then reducing a phase difference above one cycle.
questions.misconception: Inverting the ratio of separation to wavelength

explanation.body:
$v = f\lambda$: $24 = 15\lambda$, so $\lambda = 1.6\ \mathrm{m}$.

Phase difference $= \dfrac{2.0}{1.6} = 1.25$ cycles.

A whole cycle adds nothing, so the two points 2.0 m apart have a phase difference of a quarter of a cycle.

perOption.A: Only true if the separation were a whole number of wavelengths.
perOption.B: Correct. 1.25 cycles is equivalent to 0.25 cycle.
perOption.C: Would need a separation of an odd number of half-wavelengths.
perOption.D: Uses $\lambda/d = 1.6/2.0$ instead of $d/\lambda$.

questions.difficultyReason: Must identify the full repeating unit in a complex waveform before using the time-base.
questions.misconception: Taking the time between any two pulses as the period

explanation.body:
Look for the minimum pattern that repeats: the distance between two successive tall peaks is 5 cm.

$T = (5\ \mathrm{cm})(2.00\ \mathrm{ms\,cm^{-1}}) = 10\ \mathrm{ms}$, so $f = \frac{1}{10\times10^{-3}} = 100\ \mathrm{Hz}$.

perOption.A: Takes two full repeats (10 cm) as one period.
perOption.B: Correct. Period 5 cm = 10 ms.
perOption.C: Uses 4 cm as the period, not the full repeating pattern.
perOption.D: Takes 2.5 cm (e.g. tall peak to small peak) as the period, missing that the pattern repeats only every 5 cm.

questions.stem: A beam of plane-polarised light of intensity I is incident normally onto a polariser which has its polarising axis parallel to the incident beam. A second beam of plane-polarised light of intensity I is incident normally onto the same polariser but with its plane of polarisation perpendicular to the polarising axis of the polariser. Both beams of light arrived in phase to each other. The angle of polarisation for the polariser is rotated to $45^{\mathrm{o}}$. What is the intensity of the emergent beam?
questions.stemText: A beam of plane-polarised light of intensity I is incident normally onto a polariser which has its polarising axis parallel to the incident beam. A second beam of plane-polarised light of intensity I is incident normally onto the same polariser but with its plane of polarisation perpendicular to the polarising axis of the polariser. Both beams of light arrived in phase to each other. The angle of polarisation for the polariser is rotated to 45o. What is the intensity of the emergent beam? A 0.250 I B 0.500 I C I D 2 I

appearances.originalFile: grail:14610 YIJC 2024 JC2 PRELIM H2 Phy P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Unusual combination of Malus' law with coherent superposition of amplitudes.
questions.misconception: Adding intensities instead of amplitudes for coherent waves

explanation.body:
After the polariser is rotated to $45^\circ$, each emergent beam has amplitude $A' = A\cos45^\circ$.

Since the two beams arrive in phase, they superpose: total amplitude $= 2A' = 2A\cos45^\circ = \sqrt{2}A$.

Since $I \propto A^2$: $\frac{I_E}{I} = \left(\frac{\sqrt{2}A}{A}\right)^2 = 2$, so $I_E = 2I$.

perOption.A: Applies $\cos^2 45^\circ$ twice or halves the single-beam result.
perOption.B: Considers only one beam passing through ($I\cos^2 45^\circ$).
perOption.C: Adds the two transmitted intensities ($0.5I + 0.5I$) instead of adding amplitudes of the in-phase beams.
perOption.D: Correct. Coherent in-phase amplitudes add: $(\sqrt{2}A)^2 = 2A^2$.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires finding the incident angle at the inserted filter and applying Malus’ law twice.

explanation.body: Zero initial transmission means the incident polarisation is perpendicular to the first filter's transmission axis. perOption.B: Correct.
